title: Matrix Definitions & Operations
description: Square, triangular, diagonal matrices; transpose; row/column vectors; basic multiplication

questions.prompt: A matrix with the same number of rows and columns is called a _____ matrix.
explanations: Rectangular describes any matrix — not specific enough.
Diagonal is a special type of square matrix.
Triangular is also a special type of square matrix.

questions.prompt: True or False: Every diagonal matrix is also a square matrix.
explanations: A diagonal matrix has entries only on the main diagonal, which requires an equal number of rows and columns — so it must be square.

questions.prompt: True or False: Every square matrix is also a diagonal matrix.
explanations: A square matrix can have nonzero entries anywhere — only those with zeros off the diagonal are diagonal matrices.

questions.prompt: The transpose $A^T$ of a matrix $A$ is formed by:
choices: Replacing each entry with its reciprocal
Moving every entry to the opposite corner
explanations: Multiplying by $-1$ gives the negative of a matrix, not the transpose.
Replacing with reciprocals is not a standard matrix operation.
Only the main diagonal entries stay fixed under transposition — others move to their mirror position.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is a $3 \times 5$ matrix, what is the size of $A^T$?
explanations: The transpose flips dimensions — rows become columns.
Transposing does not produce a square matrix from a non-square one.
Transposing does not produce a square matrix from a non-square one.

questions.prompt: A matrix with all entries below the main diagonal equal to zero is called:
explanations: Lower triangular has zeros ABOVE the diagonal.
Diagonal requires zeros both above and below.
Symmetric requires $A = A^T$.

questions.prompt: A matrix with all entries above the main diagonal equal to zero is called:
explanations: Upper triangular has zeros BELOW the diagonal.
The identity matrix is a special square matrix — not the same thing.
The zero matrix has all entries zero, not just above the diagonal.

questions.prompt: True or False: The zero matrix is a diagonal matrix.
explanations: A diagonal matrix requires zeros off the diagonal. The zero matrix has all entries zero — the off-diagonal entries are certainly zero, so it qualifies.

questions.prompt: A matrix $A$ is called symmetric if:
explanations: $A = -A^T$ defines a skew-symmetric matrix.
$A^T = 0$ means $A$ is the zero matrix.
Diagonal matrices are symmetric, but symmetric matrices don't have to be diagonal.

questions.prompt: True or False: Every diagonal matrix is symmetric.
explanations: A diagonal matrix has $a_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$. So $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i, j$, which means $A = A^T$.

questions.prompt: A row vector is a matrix with:
explanations: That describes a column vector.
That describes a square matrix.
Entry signs are unrelated to being a row vector.

questions.prompt: A column vector with $n$ entries is a matrix of size:
explanations: $1 \times n$ is a row vector.
$n \times n$ is a square matrix.
$n \times 2$ has two columns — not a single column vector.

questions.prompt: The $(i, j)$ entry of a matrix refers to the entry in:
explanations: The convention is row first, column second.
There is no such convention.
There is no such convention.

questions.prompt: For a square matrix $A$, the main diagonal consists of the entries:
explanations: Those are the anti-diagonal entries.
The first row is not the diagonal.
The last column is not the diagonal.

questions.prompt: The transpose of a row vector is:
explanations: Transposing a $1 \times n$ row vector gives an $n \times 1$ matrix.
Only a $1 \times 1$ matrix is a scalar.
The result is $n \times 1$, not square.

questions.prompt: True or False: $(AB)^T = A^T B^T$
explanations: The correct rule reverses the order: $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$. The order matters because matrix multiplication is not commutative.

questions.prompt: The correct formula for the transpose of a product is:
explanations: This reverses the needed order reversal — $A^T B^T$ is generally not equal to $(AB)^T$.
This would mean $AB$ is symmetric, which is not generally true.
This introduces an inverse which is unrelated.

questions.prompt: True or False: $(A^T)^T = A$ for any matrix $A$.
explanations: Transposing twice returns the original matrix — transposing is its own inverse.

questions.prompt: True or False: $(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T$ when $A$ and $B$ are the same size.
explanations: Transpose distributes over addition — this property holds for all same-size matrices.

questions.prompt: Compute $AB$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}$.
explanations: That would be entry-wise multiplication, not matrix multiplication.
The result of a $1 \times 2$ times $2 \times 1$ is $1 \times 1$ — a scalar: $1(3)+2(4)=11$.
That would be the result of $BA$ (outer product), not $AB$.

questions.prompt: Compute $AB$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 4\end{bmatrix}$.
explanations: $11$ is the result of $BA$ (dot product), not $AB$.
Entry-wise — not matrix multiplication.
$A$ is $2 \times 1$ and $B$ is $1 \times 2$: columns of $A$ (1) = rows of $B$ (1), so it is defined.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a $3 \times 3$ diagonal matrix?
explanations: The entry $a_{12} = 2$ is off the diagonal — not diagonal.
The entry $a_{31} = 1$ is off the diagonal.
The nonzero entries are on the anti-diagonal, not the main diagonal.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an upper triangular matrix?
explanations: This is lower triangular — zeros are above the diagonal.
There are nonzero entries below the diagonal.
No entries are zero below the diagonal.

questions.prompt: True or False: The product of a $1 \times n$ row vector and an $n \times 1$ column vector is a scalar.
explanations: A $1 \times n$ times $n \times 1$ gives a $1 \times 1$ matrix, which is effectively a scalar (the dot product).

questions.prompt: True or False: The product of an $n \times 1$ column vector and a $1 \times n$ row vector is an $n \times n$ matrix.
explanations: An $n \times 1$ times a $1 \times n$ gives an $n \times n$ matrix — this is the outer product.

questions.prompt: A matrix $A$ is symmetric if $A = _____$.
questions.explanation: Symmetric means $A$ equals its own transpose: $A = A^T$, so $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i, j$.

questions.prompt: The transpose of a $3 \times 7$ matrix is a _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: Transposing flips the dimensions: an $m \times n$ matrix becomes $n \times m$. So $3 \times 7$ becomes $7 \times 3$.

questions.prompt: An $n \times n$ matrix with 1s on the main diagonal and 0s everywhere else is called the _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: The identity matrix $I_n$ is the matrix that acts like the number 1 for matrix multiplication: $AI = IA = A$.

questions.prompt: A matrix where all entries are zero is called the _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: The zero matrix $0$ has every entry equal to 0. It acts like the number 0 for matrix addition: $A + 0 = A$.

questions.prompt: A square matrix with zeros everywhere except possibly on the main diagonal is called a _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: A diagonal matrix has $a_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$. The diagonal entries can be any values.

questions.prompt: A matrix with a single row is called a _____ vector.
questions.explanation: A row vector is a $1 \times n$ matrix. A column vector is an $n \times 1$ matrix.

questions.prompt: The operation that flips a matrix over its main diagonal, turning rows into columns, is called the _____.
questions.explanation: The transpose $A^T$ is formed by writing the rows of $A$ as columns. Entry $(i,j)$ of $A$ becomes entry $(j,i)$ of $A^T$.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is a $4 \times 7$ matrix, how many rows does $A^T$ have?
questions.explanation: The transpose of a $4 \times 7$ matrix is $7 \times 4$. The number of rows of $A^T$ equals the number of columns of $A$.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is a $4 \times 7$ matrix, how many columns does $A^T$ have?
questions.explanation: The transpose of a $4 \times 7$ matrix is $7 \times 4$. The number of columns of $A^T$ equals the number of rows of $A$.

questions.prompt: A square matrix of size $n \times n$ has how many entries on its main diagonal?
questions.explanation: The main diagonal entries are $a_{11}, a_{22}, \ldots, a_{nn}$ — exactly $n$ entries.

questions.prompt: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 5 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(2,1)$ entry of $A$?
questions.explanation: The $(i,j)$ entry is in row $i$, column $j$. The $(2,1)$ entry is row 2, column 1: $-1$.

questions.prompt: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 5 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^T$?
questions.explanation: The $(i,j)$ entry of $A^T$ equals the $(j,i)$ entry of $A$. So $(1,2)$ of $A^T$ = $(2,1)$ of $A$ = $-1$.

questions.prompt: How many entries are in a $3 \times 4$ matrix?
questions.explanation: A $3 \times 4$ matrix has $3 \times 4 = 12$ entries.

questions.prompt: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&5&0\\0&0&-3\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(2,2)$ entry?
questions.explanation: Row 2, column 2 of this diagonal matrix is $5$.

questions.prompt: Compute the $(1,1)$ entry of $AB$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}1\\4\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.explanation: $(1,1)$ entry of $AB$ = row 1 of $A$ dotted with column 1 of $B$ = $2(1) + 3(4) = 2 + 12 = 14$.

questions.prompt: Compute the $(2,2)$ entry of $AB$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.explanation: $(2,2)$ entry = row 2 of $A$ dotted with column 2 of $B$ = $3(1) + 4(0) = 3$.

questions.prompt: Which of these matrices is lower triangular?
explanations: This is upper triangular — zeros are below the diagonal.
The $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ is actually both, but choice B is the clearest lower triangular example.
The $(1,2)$ entry is 2, which is above the diagonal — not lower triangular.

questions.prompt: True or False: If $A$ is symmetric then $A$ must be square.
explanations: Symmetric means $A = A^T$. For this to hold, $A$ and $A^T$ must be the same size — $A$ must be $n \times n$.

questions.prompt: If $A = \begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&5\end{bmatrix}$, is $A$ symmetric?
explanations: $a_{12} = 1 = a_{21}$, so $A = A^T$. This matrix is symmetric.

questions.prompt: If $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$, what is $A^T$?
explanations: That is the matrix reflected along the other diagonal, not the transpose.
That is $A$ itself — $A$ is not symmetric so $A \neq A^T$.
That is $-A$, not $A^T$.

questions.prompt: Which of these matrices is lower triangular?
explanations: This is upper triangular — zeros below the diagonal, not above.
Nonzero entries appear both above and below the diagonal.
The $(1,2)$ entry is 2, which is above the diagonal — not lower triangular.

questions.prompt: Scalar multiplication $cA$ multiplies:
choices: Only the diagonal entries of $A$ by $c$
Only the first row of $A$ by $c$
explanations: Scalar multiplication affects every entry, not just the diagonal.
Scalar multiplication changes values of entries, not the size of the matrix.
Every entry is scaled, not just the first row.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix and $c = 2$, what is the size of $cA$?
explanations: Scalar multiplication does not change the dimensions.
Scalar multiplication does not change the dimensions.
Scalar multiplication does not change the dimensions.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition $A + B$ is performed by:
choices: Adding all entries of $B$ to the first row of $A$
explanations: That describes matrix multiplication, not addition.
Appending columns would change the size — not what addition does.
Addition affects every corresponding entry equally.

questions.prompt: True or False: The zero matrix has all entries equal to zero.
explanations: The zero matrix is defined as the matrix where every single entry equals zero.

questions.prompt: The $(i,j)$ entry of $A^T$ equals which entry of $A$?
explanations: That would mean $A^T = A$, which is only true for symmetric matrices.
Transposing swaps row and column indices — nothing else.
Transposing swaps row and column indices — nothing else.

questions.prompt: True or False: Scalar multiplication changes the size of a matrix.
explanations: Scalar multiplication scales every entry but leaves the number of rows and columns unchanged.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is $3 \times 4$ and $B$ is $3 \times 4$, then $A + B$ is a _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: Matrix addition does not change the size — the result has the same dimensions as the operands.

questions.prompt: True or False: A symmetric matrix must have equal entries that mirror across the main diagonal.
explanations: Symmetric means $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i$ and $j$ — entries mirror across the main diagonal by definition.

questions.prompt: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(1,2)$ entry of $A + B$?
Let $c = 3$ and $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\0&4\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(2,2)$ entry of $cA$?
Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(2,1)$ entry of $A^T$?
questions.explanation: The $(2,1)$ entry of $A^T$ equals the $(1,2)$ entry of $A$, which is $3$.

questions.prompt: Compute the $(1,2)$ entry of $AB$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.explanation: $(AB)_{12}$ = row 1 of $A$ dotted with column 2 of $B$ = $1(1) + 2(3) = 1 + 6 = 7$.
